edge_720.relationship: Environmental perspectives on city–hinterland connections, assessed in period by an urban historian as a contribution to urban history (1991–92)
edge_720.evidence_note: In-period evidence: the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (open PDF, text layer read). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context', and that Cronon 'has, perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward from its current relegation as a kind of assumed stage set for monographs on local occurrences in cities' (p. 491). Of the premise that 'to really understand how and why cities developed, one must study how they organized their hinterlands', he writes: 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates the explanatory power of this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). He also finds that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon’s response: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change'; 'Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field, setting the process of urbanization in a broader context that is as important to urban historians as it is to environmental ones' (p. 520). The arrow rests on one book, one urban historian’s in-period assessment and the author’s reply; it does not claim that urban history as a field adopted environmental questions. Context only, not support for the claim: Cronon’s 1993 ASEH address names Joel Tarr’s 'many studies of pollution and waste streams' (p. 3, n. 6) and cites Melosi’s Garbage in the Cities (n. 24). cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. Cronon’s own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.131).

edge_892.relationship: Settler colonialism as the frame for a history of anthropology (1999)

edge_901.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995)
edge_901.evidence_note: Cronon’s own in-period statements. Changes in the Land (1983), ch. 1 'The View from Walden', read in full in an unpaginated web transcription (page numbers not verified): 'The replacement of Indians by predominantly European populations in New England was as much an ecological as a cultural revolution'; 'An ecological history begins by assuming a dynamic and changing relationship between environment and culture, one as apt to produce contradictions as continuities. Moreover, it assumes that the interactions of the two are dialectical'; 'The choice is not between two landscapes, one with and one without a human influence; it is between two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'; 'The pig was not merely a pig but a creature bound among other things to the fence, the dandelion, and a very special definition of property'; a 'world capitalist system' draws people 'into trade and market relations which lie well beyond the boundaries of their local ecosystems'. He sets this against species-transfer accounts 'as Alfred Crosby and William H. McNeill have done', which are 'bound to be incomplete', and against functionalist ecological anthropology, which risks 'a static and ahistorical view'. In 1992 he calls Nature’s Metropolis 'a natural sequel' to that book, which 'described a comparable set of environmental changes that occurred in New England as that region became linked to London’s markets' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 517). 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993): the lesson 'When people buy and sell things in a market, they link together ecosystems and encourage change' is 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14, citing Changes in the Land, Nature’s Metropolis and 'Kennecott Journey'); 'The chief moral of my own version of environmental history is the one I tried to embed in the title of my book Changes in the Land. To live as human beings on this planet is to change the world around us' (p. 19); 'the material history of environmental change is simultaneously a spiritual history of human consciousness and a political economic history of human society' (p. 19); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14), held together with the claim that 'the natural world exists quite apart from what we believe about it' (p. 15). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 33): 'The special task of environmental historians is to tell stories that carry us back and forth across the boundary between people and nature to reveal just how culturally constructed that boundary is—and how dependent upon natural systems it remains.' 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995, author’s reflow p. 1): wilderness is 'quite profoundly a human creation'. A contribution, not a founding: he makes the claim for materialist analysis that tries 'to finesse a full-blown determinism' on behalf of the field ('One important contribution of environmental history', 1993, p. 13), and places the field among the 'new' histories of the 1960s (p. 2). Contested in period: Danbom (1992) reads Nature’s Metropolis for its 'environmental moralism' (p. 503) and as 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506); Cronon answers 'I see no pure heroes or pure villains in the stories I tell' (p. 522). His 1990 JAH response to Worster is unread. The 2003 afterword (pp. 182–185: property analysis learned from anthropology, economics and legal theory; his own criticism of schematic capitalism and source asymmetry) is a later reading. edge_342 (anthropology → environment) and edge_343 (environment → culture) stay: they record anthropology as a resource and environmental history’s contribution to cultural history; this arrow is his own framework.

edge_903.relationship: Narrative bounded by evidence, ecology and the community of scholars: an environmental historian’s answer to postmodern critiques of narrative (1992)
edge_903.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative', JAH 78:4 (March 1992), author-hosted copy in journal pagination (pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read). Writing about narrative, 'we cannot avoid encountering the postmodernist assault on narrative, which calls into question not just the stories we tell but the deeper purpose that motivated us in the first place' (p. 1349). The argument is meant for all historians: 'I am urging historians to acknowledge storytelling as the necessary core even of longue durée histories … Environmental history is but one example of these, and most of my arguments apply just as readily to the others' (p. 1349, n. 5). 'I, like most practicing historians, am only willing to follow the postmodernists so far'; 'My goal throughout has been to acknowledge the immense power of narrative while still defending the past (and nature) as real things to which our storytelling must somehow conform lest it cease being history altogether' (p. 1372). Three bounds: 'our stories cannot contravene known facts about the past' and 'our stories must make ecological sense' (p. 1372); 'We write as members of communities' (p. 1373). 'To just that extent, nature coauthors our stories' (p. 1373). Against 'an endless postmodernist deconstruction of texts that fails to ground itself in history, in community, in politics, and finally in the moral problem of living on earth' he asserts 'the virtues of narrative' (p. 1374), and he asks environmental historians for 'not just stories about nature, but stories about stories about nature' (p. 1375). He reads with Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form and with Novick (nn. 6, 7, 43), and credits Richard White with the argument about criticism (n. 46). The 1993 address restates it: historical wisdom 'usually comes in the form of parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16). This is his own text; no in-period reading that places the essay in the postmodernism debate was read.

edge_904.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990)
edge_904.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'.

anthropology.label: Anthropology & ethnography
anthropology.description: Ethnographic observation, comparison, historical reconstruction and interpretation generate different accounts of social life. Exchanges with historians involve particular works and methods; colonial knowledge, research authority and the representation of cultures are contested within and beyond the discipline.
anthropology.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct stages include Tylor and Frazer, Boasian historical particularism, and later interpretive anthropology associated with Geertz. These do not form one continuous theory.

anthropology.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

anticolonial.description: Recasts empire through slavery, resistance, liberation, and colonized peoples’ historical agency. environment.label: Environmental history
environment.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts. Dust Bowl debates distinguish agricultural capitalism, technology and soils, federal intervention, regional scale and household survival; primary criticism and later social history complicate a single causal summary.
environment.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

environment.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995), reviewed by Carruthers (1996); The Kruger National Park (1995), prologue and epilogue

gender.label: Gender history
gender.description: Examines gender as a historically changing organization of social relations, identities and power. Research on work, family, masculinity, bodies and colonial settings connects gender to class, race and other relations without reducing these to one framework. Some feminist historians develop and criticize British Marxist social history; this is one route among several.

indigenous.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

science.label: History of science
science.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches
science.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
science.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

cdn_working_class.label: Canadian working-class history
cdn_working_class.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · selected later works
cdn_working_class.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
cdn_working_class.representative_figures_and_works: Logan, Trade Unions in Canada (1948); Abella, Nationalism, Communism, and Canadian Labour (1973); Bercuson, Confrontation at Winnipeg (1974); Copp, The Anatomy of Poverty (1974); Labour/Le Travailleur (1976); Palmer, A Culture in Conflict (1979); Finkel, Business and Social Reform in the Thirties (1979); Kealey, Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980); McNaught, Bercuson and Kealey (1981); Kealey and Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be (1982); Struthers, No Fault of Their Own (1983); Palmer, Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992); Heron, Working in Steel (1988); Rouillard, Histoire du syndicalisme au Québec (1989); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Kealey, Workers and Canadian History (1995); Heron, The Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998); Morton and Sangster in Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000). Later: High, Industrial Sunset (2003); McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008); Burrill (2019); Finkel on Palmer (2021).
cdn_working_class.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) are treated mainly in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his main entry is Liberal order framework.

native_newcomer.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
native_newcomer.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · selected later works
native_newcomer.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.

Later: Rutherdale (2002), Brownlie (2003), Raibmon (2005), Podruchny (2006), Lutz, Makúk (2008). Critics and alternatives: Sioui (1989), Paul, We Were Not the Savages (1993; 2000 edition), Stevenson [Wheeler], “The Othering of Indigenous History” (1998), LaRocque (1999); in the US, Fixico (2009) and S. A. Miller (2009).
native_newcomer.scope_note: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework, and whether any adopts it was not checked; and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with Settler colonialism.

settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
settler_colonialism.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) and “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. (2005); Veracini, Settler Colonialism (2010) and Settler Colonial Studies (2011). Read with Coulthard (2014), A. Simpson (2014), L. B. Simpson (2011, 2017), Byrd (2011) and Tuck and Yang (2012). Canadian historiography: Carter (1990, 2008), Harris (2002, 2004, 2020), Perry (2001), Regan (2010), Daschuk (2013), Battell Lowman and Barker (2015), Burrill (2019). Critiques: Macoun and Strakosch (2013), Rowse (2014), Kauanui (2016), Greer (2019), Shoemaker (2019), Konishi (2019), Garba and Sorentino (2020).
settler_colonialism.scope_note: A selective research field whose theoretical consolidation came mostly after 2000; the entry covers its roots through 2000 and cites selected later works as readings. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.

william_cronon.label: William Cronon
william_cronon.date_label: Changes in the Land 1983 · Nature’s Metropolis 1991 · “The Trouble with Wilderness” 1995
william_cronon.description: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'.
william_cronon.representative_figures_and_works: William Cronon (b. 1954); Changes in the Land: Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England (1983); “Modes of Prophecy and Production: Placing Nature in History” (JAH 1990); Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991); “Kennecott Journey: The Paths out of Town” (1992); “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (JAH 1992); “The Uses of Environmental History” (1993); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995). Readings: the Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response (1992); Sessions’s reply on wilderness (1996); his own afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).

He places environmental history among the 'new' histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' (1993, p. 2), names Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne as practitioners (pp. 2–3), footnotes lessons to Crosby, Richard White, McEvoy and others (pp. 8–10), and echoes Leopold (n. 11). His 2003 afterword, McNeill (2003) and Canadian uses after 2000 are later readings.

donald_worster.label: Donald Worster
donald_worster.date_label: Nature's Economy 1977 · Dust Bowl 1979 · Rivers of Empire 1985 · 'Transformations of the Earth' 1990
donald_worster.description: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'.
donald_worster.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Worster (b. 1941); Nature's Economy: The Roots of Ecology (1977); Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); Rivers of Empire: Water, Aridity, and the Growth of the American West (1985); 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', in The Ends of the Earth (1988); 'Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History', Journal of American History (1990), reprinted in The Wealth of Nature (1993). Readings: Merchant's round-table response (1990); Cronon, 'A Place for Stories' (1992); Hennessey's review of Rivers of Empire (1987); McDean (1986).
donald_worster.scope_note: This entry presents the three-level model in Worster's 1988 wording, checked in an abridged reprint and by full-text search of the 1988 edition, and the 1990 essay in his own 1993 reprint; the Journal of American History pages of 1990 were not reachable and are given only where another writer cites them (Isenberg 2013). Dust Bowl and Rivers of Empire are quoted at the pages given by Cronon (1992) and Hennessey (1987), with the wording confirmed by search of the original editions. He is not presented as the founder of the field or the sole author of the scheme: he grounds the idea in Aldo Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history', and Arthur McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. The scheme was contested at once: Merchant (1990) added gender and 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction', Cronon (1992) treated Dust Bowl as a declensionist narrative, and McDean (1986) criticised its generalisation across the Plains. The 1990 objections of White and Cronon in the round table are known here only through Isenberg (2013), a later reading.

capitalismdebates.label: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation
capitalismdebates.date_label: Capitalism and Slavery 1944 · Dobb–Sweezy 1950 · Brenner debate 1976–85 · Wrigley 1988 · de Vries 1994 · The Great Divergence 2000 · Allen and The Enlightened Economy 2009 · Empire of Cotton 2014 · Hilt 2017 · Burnard and Riello 2020
capitalismdebates.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.
strands.works: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb, Science & Society 14:2 (1950): 134–167; Takahashi (1952); Merrington, 'Town and Country in the Transition to Capitalism' (NLR, 1975); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976); see marx/transition and economic/marxist

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.
strands.works: Wood, The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), replies (2002); McAuley (2001)

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.
strands.works: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884); Crafts and Harley (1992); Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper; EHR 1992); de Vries (JEH 1994), pp. 249–251; see historicalecon/british_teaching

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term he and van Nederveen Meerkerk trace to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley questioned whether the Industrial Enlightenment explained economic change or largely redescribed it (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage. The article sets it 'directly counter' to Allen's argument (pp. 60–61), as their 2014 essay had argued from British workers' human capital against his high wages. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong explained divergence by political fragmentation and war (2011, as Ma's review reports and Wong restated in 2016); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.
strands.works: Wong, China Transformed (1997); Frank, ReOrient (1998); Landes, The Wealth and Poverty of Nations (1998); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000); Frank's review (2001); Goldstone (2002); Brenner and Isett (2002); Mokyr (2002; 2012); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Vries (2009; 2013); Parthasarathi (2011); Rosenthal and Wong (2011); Allen et al. (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021); see global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.
strands.works: Johnson, River of Dark Dreams (2013); Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told (2014); Beckert, Empire of Cotton (2014); Beckert and Rockman (eds), Slavery’s Capitalism (2016); Olmstead and Rhode (AHA 2017; EEH 2018); Hilt (JEH 2017); Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020); Regele (2023)
